articles.title: GM just did 34,000 years of battery testing in less than a month. Here’s how
articles.description: Developing new EV battery technology takes years of research. General Motors, for example, says it’s put a decade of effort into lithium manganese-rich, or LMR, batteries, which aren’t yet in any of their vehicles on the road. But recently, the automaker says it made a big leap in that work. Using computer modeling, GM was able to virtually test more than 300,000 LMR battery pack configurations, advancing from first concept to formal approval in under a month. That represents more than 300 million CPU hours, which would take a typical computer 34,000 years, while running 24 hours a day, to complete, according to GM. GM is leaning into artificial intelligence and virtual simulations to develop its vehicles. That not only speeds up the time to do testing, per the company, but allows it to test more options, rather than picking the best of just a few configurations. Those 300,000 formulations, for example, looked at different chemical combinations, temperature cycling, and other approaches to creating a battery cell, Sterling Anderson, GM’s chief product officer, told Fast Company. “If we had not had the luxury of some of these tools, we would have had to sample more sparsely from what was possible,” he says. Speeding up vehicle development GM is bringing this AI approach beyond battery testing and into all areas of its vehicle development, with the aim of slashing the time it takes to develop a car in half. Typically, cars are developed within a four- or five-year time frame. That allows a “limited number” of all kinds of tests, Anderson says, from wind tunnel to crash tests. “Now in the virtual world, instead of the X crash test that we could have done, or Y prototypes that could go through, we can run X times 100 and Y times 1000,” he says. GM is also working to advance its autonomous driving capabilities with real-world and virtual testing. Hundreds of data-collection vehicles are currently driving across the country collecting 1 million miles of data a month, while virtually, GM systems drive more than 3 billion simulated miles a day. By cutting vehicle development down to about two years, GM also says it can adapt more quickly to external challenges. Many car makers were counting on Biden-era EV tax credits to help their sales, for example, but then the Trump administration cut those credits. Tariffs, the war in Iran’s effect on gas prices, changing regulations, and uneasy consumer sentiments have all added uncertainty to automakers’ future product lineups, which may have been in development for years. A shorter development cycle “makes you more agile,” Anderson says. LMR batteries in the works GM wants to be the first automaker to deploy LMR batteries, and Anderson says they’re on track to make that happen. LMR batteries can have 33% more energy density than lithium iron phosphate chemistry, and use a higher amount of less-expensive minerals (like manganese) rather than more of the most expensive minerals like cobalt and nickel. That allows them to offer more range—potentially more than 400 miles—at a lower cost and lighter weight. GM is also preparing to roll out its fourth-generation EV platform, which includes not only LMR batteries but a centralized, upgraded computing system, and new electrical work. It will have 30% less wiring than GM’s current EVs and 40% fewer parts in its motors and power electronics, which make it lighter and more efficient. GM and LG Energy Solution are working on these batteries as part of a joint venture called Ultium Cells. They plan to start commercial production of the LMR battery cells in the U.S. by 2028, at the Ultium Cells facility in Spring Hill, Tennessee.

articles.title: Tech-savvy STEM students prone to letting AI do their thinking for them, study shows
articles.description: CORVALLIS, Ore. – University students with traits coveted in STEM fields are also the ones most prone to relying on artificial intelligence to the detriment of their cognitive skills, according to a new study by scientists at Oregon State University. Researchers in OSU’s colleges of Engineering and Liberal Arts offer suggestions for breaking what they call “the self-reinforcing cognitive debt cycle” stemming from routine AI dependence. The study led by computer science graduate student Rudrajit “Rudy” Choudhuri indicates that without corrective action by educators and AI designers, thinking skills will steadily decline amid an illusion of increased efficiency.“Our findings make you rethink what kind of AI literacy is useful after all,” he said. Choudhuri and doctoral advisor Anita Sarma teamed up with Margaret Burnett, distinguished professor of computer science, and Christopher Sanchez, associate professor of psychological science, to analyze survey data from 299 STEM students representing five North American universities. The analysis, published in Information and Software Technology, reveals a feedback loop: The routine use of generative AI serves to weaken students’ intellectual habits, which leads them to lean on AI even more, further diminishing their thinking skills.“The most surprising finding was that the ‘AI-savvy’ ones, who you might think do significantly better in STEM careers, are actually spinning themselves deeper into the AI dependence spiral,” Choudhuri said. “The choices educators and AI designers make now will shape not only what students learn, but how they learn to think.”The researchers note that the “cognitive laziness” associated with an over-reliance on AI is explained at least in part by evolution. Our ancestors who learned the skillful use of intuitive, automatic and low-effort “system 1” thinking were able to outcompete those who overapplied “system 2” thinking, which is deliberate, controlled and effortful.“System 1 is what delivers the rapid answer to 2 + 2 = ? or completes the phrase ‘bread and _____,” Choudhuri said. “System 2 is invoked when you calculate 17 × 24 or evaluate a complex argument. System 2 is lazy. It avoids effort whenever System 1 can provide a plausible solution. It’s what psychologists call the law of least effort, which is a pervasive tendency to accept the path of least cognitive resistance.”Basically, human ancestors who conserved their mental energy for actual threats survived whereas those who performed exhaustive analyses prior to every decision didn’t.“Today we make shopping lists rather than rely on memory, let calculators do our arithmetic and use GPS instead of reading maps,” Sarma added. “Generative AI tools tend to amplify this sort of trend because they deliver fluent, confident support on demand. That means interacting with AI is more about choosing from outputs rather than thinking by doing.”Though choosing instead of thinking can create a compelling sense of progress via time savings, they said, it’s problematic for learning. That’s particularly true in STEM education, where students need “desirable difficulties” – slow, painstaking cognitive work that builds intuition and transferable skills. In the survey, students who trusted and routinely used generative AI reported significantly lower cognitive engagement.“The types of skills that students are farming out to AI actually put them in a hole when it comes to developing skills that are genuinely needed,” Sanchez said. “In short, they are not using AI as an assistant but as more of a substitute for actually engaging with learning a topic.”The scientists suggest some ways for students to build these cognitive skills, including:Increasing the intrinsic reward of cognitive engagement by designing coursework as opportunities for exploration through storytelling, game playing or puzzle solving. Alternating between AI-assisted and independent work. For example, students might first problem solve with help from AI, then be required to independently critique, debug/repair, verify and adapt that contribution to their project requirements without AI during a supervised lab. Combining these approaches with in-class assessments and/or collaborative/group activities to further reinforce engagement by leveraging social accountability. Designing generative AI systems as “bicycles for the mind.” Bikes amplify physical efficiency while requiring the rider’s active control; designed as mind-bicycles, AI would amplify cognition via critique, counter argument and provocation while keeping humans responsible for exploration, steering and judgment.“Absent intervention, STEM education runs the risk of cultivating a generation of students unwilling and/or unable to exercise their capacity for reflection, understanding and critical thinking,” Burnett said. “If routine reliance on AI changes students’ willingness to engage in effortful thinking, many may enter professional life without having developed the intellectual habits that earlier generations gained through practice.”The USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture and the National Science Foundation supported this study.

articles.title: Experimental mRNA vaccine cuts risk melanoma returns by 42%
articles.description: When the news arrived in August that what could be the first personalized mRNA cancer vaccine had succeeded in a late-stage clinical trial in melanoma, oncologists and the public alike were exhilarated. And that was before its makers had even disclosed just how well the therapy worked.

articles.title: A house ages alongside its occupants, according to researcher
articles.description: Flemish people are very attached to their homes and generally wish to stay there for as long as possible. However, many homes were not designed to be lived in for a lifetime. Architect and researcher Sander Lambrix has analyzed the relationship between our homes and our well-being as we grow older. His conclusion: a home is much more than just a physical environment, whether or not it is suited to an aging body. People and their homes are deeply connected on an emotional level.

articles.title: Music can enhance the flavor of your food
articles.description: The moment we take a sip of our morning coffee or our first bite of lunch, the brain begins interpreting what we taste. Is it sweet? Sour? Or something else entirely? But the brain does not create flavor based solely on signals from the tongue. That is the finding of a new study from the Department of Food Science, published in Scientific Reports.

articles.title: Are 'mega-Earths' real? Stellar activity may explain these oversized rocky worlds
articles.description: A new study suggests that some of the heaviest rocky planets ever reported may not be as heavy as they look. These so-called 'mega-Earths,' rocky planets weighing more than about 10 Earths, could be an illusion created by activity on their host stars. The paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 8.

articles.title: Legal encounters may offer overlooked opportunities for suicide prevention, analysis suggests
articles.description: Picture a forlorn man walking into a lawyer's office after his marriage has collapsed. The bank is threatening foreclosure, and his finances are in tatters. His problems may be legal on paper, but in person they can look far more complicated: panic, shame or the numb resignation of someone who can no longer imagine a way out. He did not come for counseling, and his lawyer is not a therapist. Still, the attorney may be sitting beside him at the worst moment of his life—with a chance to help before despair slides into tragedy.

articles.title: Raised brows and a slow blink make speakers look more confident
articles.description: Researchers studying facial movements have found that it's not just what you say, but what your face does when you say it, that counts when it comes to appearing confident when answering a question.

articles.title: Algae-powered soft robot arm uses light to grasp and lift small objects
articles.description: Tiny underwater algae sway gently in the current. All of a sudden, a light shines on them and they form robotlike arms that start to pick up small rocks and put them in floating baskets. Sounds like science fiction, but researchers from Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have created a small soft robot arm covered with minuscule algae that can grasp and lift objects. And it's powered by light. This next step in biotechnology has been published in Nature Communications.

articles.title: Good growth: Innovate Cambridge Summit 2026
articles.description: Good growth: Innovate Cambridge Summit 2026 Sarah Fell Thu, 10/22/2026 - 09:56 New analysis from Cambridge Innovation Capital (CIC), published ahead of the Summit, showed the average equity raised per deal across both life sciences and deep tech has increased five-fold in the last decade, with Cambridge-based early-stage companies having raised £9.1 billion in that period. Taking leadership in innovation Professor Deborah Prentice, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Cambridge reflected on what makes Cambridge such a thriving innovation economy and the importance of taking a proactive and global leadership role in driving innovation that works for everyone: “There are three ways in which Cambridge takes leadership: through research excellence, by acting as one ecosystem and through our partnerships with other places and organisations.” These themes were echoed by speakers throughout the day, including Mayor Paul Bristow, Peter Freeman (Chair of the Greater Cambridge Development Corporation) and Roland Sinker (Chair of the Inclusive Innovation and Growth Review, University of Cambridge) with a recurring focus on breakthrough research, ambitious partnerships and a shared sense of purpose across the ecosystem. Strengthening the life sciences ecosystem Following GSK’s recent announcement that it will be moving its R&D headquarters to Cambridge in 2029, Chief Scientific Officer, Tony Wood spoke about the increasing need for collaboration in the life sciences and that by moving to Cambridge GSK will be able to create more opportunities to achieve breakthroughs in drug discovery and patient care. Global ambitions for quantum computing John Aston, Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Research at the University of Cambridge led a discussion considering the UK’s global leadership role in spearheading the development and application of quantum computing. The University’s partnership with IonQ, which next year will bring the UK’s first commercial scale quantum computer to Cambridge, combined with the University’s research strengths in both quantum and its potential applications, underpinned by the ecosystem’s strength in supporting commercialisation, means that Cambridge is uniquely placed to play a national – and global - leadership role. City partnerships: Manchester and Cambridge Faye Holland (Director, Cambridge x Manchester Partnership) described the increasing success of the partnership between Cambridge and Manchester in combining the regions’ complementary strengths to increase the UK’s global competitiveness. The pioneering model for this cross-city approach is now being championed by government and adopted by other city partnerships across the UK. Keeping jobs and know-how in the UK How to create the right conditions for start-ups to grow, scale and stay in the UK was explored, and the creation of a new task force announced by Pascal Levensohn (Chair of Cambridge Innovation Hub Global Advisory Board) to take forward a new approach (outlined in a white paper published ahead of the Summit) to keeping a company’s footprint in the UK even if it is acquired internationally. The Summit also heard from some of Cambridge’s most successful start-ups including Nyobolt and T-Therapeutics (both of which spun out of the University with support from Cambridge Enterprise) as well as Pragmatic Semiconductors, Cambridge Aerospace and CuspAI. Widening opportunities Ensuring that innovation-led growth benefits everyone who lives and works in Cambridge and the wider region was a central and recurring theme. Included, a new initiative to create more opportunities for young people in Greater Cambridge was announced at the Summit, with organisations present asked to contribute opportunities such as workplace visits, work experience and mentoring. Accelerating the energy transition In a parallel session, leaders from across the Cambridge cleantech ecosystem discussed accelerating the UK's clean energy transition. Hosted by DESNZ, Innovate Cambridge and Cambridge Zero, and chaired by Professor Emily Shuckburgh, Chief Scientific Adviser at DESNZ, the session brought together experts from industry, investment, academia and government. Discussions explored the opportunities and barriers to scaling cleantech innovation and commercialisation, alongside the role that innovation clusters such as Cambridge can play in addressing national clean energy challenges. Vice-Chancellor Deborah Prentice speaking at Innovate Cambridge Summit 2026 Yes

articles.title: Taiwan issues warnings as Typhoon Champi nears
articles.description: A powerful typhoon headed toward Taiwan on Thursday, triggering the cancellation of dozens of flights and prompting warnings for locals to prepare for heavy rain, strong winds and giant waves.

articles.title: Baby manta rays hunker down close to coasts before facing the open ocean's dangers
articles.description: Giant manta rays can grow up to nine meters (30 feet) long with a disk size of seven meters (23 feet) across and weigh up to 2,000 kg (4,400 pounds). This size leaves them with very few natural enemies once they reach adulthood at around eight to 10 years old. But giant manta ray babies, called pups, cannot rely on their size to protect them from predators that live in the open ocean, including several species of shark and orcas.

articles.title: Illegal fishing is thriving in African waters—a satellite system could help change that
articles.description: A patrol boat off the coast of Gabon intercepted three trawlers in July 2026, inside the Grand Sud Reserve. This is one of West and Central Africa's largest marine reserves, where industrial trawling is banned. None of the trawlers held a valid license. The patrol found them because analysts at the nonprofit Global Fishing Watch had studied satellite data and worked out where to look.

articles.title: More young people are being recruited as 'money mules' by organized crime groups, new analysis reveals
articles.description: More than 8,900 people aged under 30 were arrested for money laundering offenses in England and Wales between 2020 and 2025. That's more than six in 10 of all money laundering arrests recorded during the period.

articles.title: A rock plunged 90 kilometers into Earth and revealed something unexpected
articles.description: Scientists discovered a rock in Papua New Guinea that plunged more than 90 kilometers beneath Earth's surface, revealing a bizarre temperature pattern that challenges established theories of Earth's interior. The unexpected shift from unusually hot to relatively cold conditions could transform our understanding of tectonic plate movements, earthquakes, and volcanoes.

articles.title: Australian Zoo Plays Matchmaker for Giant Birds, and Big Green Eggs Are Proof
articles.description: A southern cassowary at the Adelaide Zoo has laid eggs there for the first time in 34 years, after a carefully managed breeding process.

articles.title: Student motivation and responsibility shown to be key to tackling bullying in physical education
articles.description: Physical education has traditionally been one of the most eagerly awaited classes of the school day, since it lets students get out of the classroom, move around and interact with their classmates in a different way—conditions that are conducive to learning values such as camaraderie and cooperation. However, the physical exposure and the dynamics of interaction, comparison and competition that the class can entail still make some students uneasy, and, in settings where bullying occurs, turn it into a potentially unsafe space.

articles.title: Private business fortunes reveal overlooked source of wealth and inequality in America
articles.description: A majority of Americans blame billionaires for the nation's ever-growing income and wealth divide. But economists Eric Zwick and Owen Zidar say there's a much larger but little-known cadre of very rich folks who may be even more important in closing the gap.

articles.title: A critical flaw affecting 70% of all websites has the cybersecurity world panicked
articles.description: Millions of websites and online tools have relied on the PHP language for decades – but newly disclosed bugs could let hackers easily take them over.

articles.title: Virus that sickens cows, kills deer still rare in New York state—for now
articles.description: An insect-driven disease that causes high mortality in white-tailed deer and mimics the symptoms of foot-and-mouth disease in cattle is still rare in New York state, but the warming climate may increase its future spread.

articles.description: What happens when a young student gets a low math score? A parent may say, "Math has never been your strength." A teacher might write "careless" beside a calculation.

articles.description: Although the Euclid space telescope is equipped with instruments to observe distant galaxies, it recently detected a comet that was previously unknown. Located in the solar system, it could take thousands of years to orbit the Sun.

articles.title: Japan's expensive funerals and declining birthrates are transforming ancestral traditions
articles.description: Whenever I drive amid the mazelike bustle of Tokyo's Shuto Expressway, where approximately 1 million vehicles transit daily, I see billboard advertisements for all manner of businesses: dentists, hotels, car and tire companies, and affordable funerals. Lots and lots of funerals.

articles.title: Webb Captures Stars in the Early Stages of Life in a Nearby Stellar Nursery
articles.description: This Webb infrared image, released on October 6th, 2026, shows the star-forming region NGC 7129, about 3,300 light-years from Earth. The central star, LkHα 234, is a young star of 5–8 solar masses whose outflows have cleared a cavity about 3.5 light-years across. On the right side of the region, younger protostars shoot jets of very hot material that create shocks in the surrounding gas.

articles.title: New lab to become centre for investigating uplands
articles.description: The research facility in Penrith will also help train the next generation of environmental scientists.

articles.title: Reconstructing 16,000 years of summer temperature change in the Western Balkans
articles.description: Researchers at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) have reconstructed approximately 16,000 years of summer temperature changes from sediments collected at Lake Prokoško in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The findings show how the Western Balkans responded to rapid climate changes at the end of the last glacial period, how warmer and cooler phases unfolded during the Holocene, and how the impact of human land use became increasingly pronounced.

articles.title: AI designs functional enzyme components that could help expand drug discovery
articles.description: New active ingredients for drugs to treat infections, cancer or other serious diseases are often based on substances originally discovered in microorganisms, plants or other living organisms. Producing or improving such active ingredients in a targeted manner using microorganisms is often challenging because the underlying biological processes are extremely complex.

articles.title: A scuff on your bag, a dent in your mug—and suddenly it feels like time for a new one
articles.description: Imagine you have a bag you really like. It felt like "the one" when you bought it. Over time, it starts to look worn. There are some scuffs on it. Nothing is actually wrong with the bag, and it still works exactly as it should. Yet, once you notice those imperfections, you start thinking about buying a new one to replace it.

articles.title: Breaking through the 'fog of war': Game-based study suggests shared boundaries can foster peace
articles.description: What causes adversaries to escalate conflicts into costly, prolonged wars even when neither side wants to fight? And in the fog of war, what might help them break that cycle and find a path to peace?
